item.title: Oil holds near 7-month highs ahead of US-Iran talks
item.description:
Oil prices hovered near their highest levels in seven months on Tuesday as markets braced for a critical round of nuclear talks between the United States and Iran, with traders weighing the risk of a military conflict that could disrupt crude supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures climbed as high as $72.50 a barrel on Monday — the highest since July 31 — before settling around $71.40, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures touched $67.28, their highest since August 4, according to Reuters. Both benchmarks held near those levels in early Wednesday trading in Asia, with Brent rising 0.64% to $71.22 and WTI gaining 0.6% to $66.05.

item.title: General Atlantic stake sale values ByteDance at $550B
item.description:
Investment firm General Atlantic is selling a stake in ByteDance in a deal that values the Chinese social media giant at $550 billion, according to a Reuters exclusive citing two people with knowledge of the matter. The proposed transaction would be the first major share sale since the Trump administration cleared the divestiture of TikTok's U.S. operations in January, and it marks a dramatic rise in the privately held company's valuation.

The $550 billion figure represents a 66% jump from an employee share buyback last year that priced ByteDance at more than $330 billion, and a 15% increase from a secondary market transaction in November that valued the company at $480 billion.

item.title: Shrinking sea ice threatens emperor penguins during moult, study finds
item.description:
Scientists studying satellite images of Antarctica have stumbled upon the first-ever observation of emperor penguin moulting colonies — and with it, a troubling new dimension to the species' struggle for survival. The discovery, published Wednesday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, reveals that shrinking sea ice is forcing the birds into increasingly crowded groups during their annual feather replacement, with potentially fatal consequences.

The findings from the British Antarctic Survey add to a growing body of evidence that climate change is pushing the world's largest penguin species toward extinction. At current rates of warming, there is a 45% chance the species will disappear by the end of the century, the survey said.

item.title: Japan's Nikkei closes at all-time high as AI rally lifts global markets
item.description: Markets around the world climbed on Wednesday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 closing at an all-time high and Europe's STOXX 600 touching a record, as a Wall Street rally fueled by renewed optimism about artificial intelligence rippled across global exchanges.

item.title: Study maps quantum effect that could enable battery-free devices
item.description:
An international team of physicists has identified how tiny imperfections and lattice vibrations inside a quantum material can be harnessed to convert ambient energy into usable electrical power, a finding that could clear the way for a new class of battery-free electronic devices.

The study, published February 24 in the journal Newton, details the mechanisms governing the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in bismuth telluride, a well-known topological insulator. The research was led by Professor Dongchen Qi from the Queensland University of Technology (QUT) School of Chemistry and Physics in Australia and Professor Xiao Renshaw Wang from Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

item.title: Largest-ever ALMA image reveals Milky Way's hidden core
item.description:
Astronomers have unveiled the largest image ever captured by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), revealing the swirling splendor of cold, star-forming gases at the center of the Milky Way in unprecedented detail. The mosaic, released Wednesday by the European Southern Observatory, spans more than 650 light-years and covers the dense clouds of gas and dust surrounding the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's core.

The image is the centerpiece of a major new dataset from ACES — the ALMA Central Molecular Zone Exploration Survey — a collaboration involving more than 160 scientists at over 70 institutions worldwide. The findings are detailed in five papers accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, with a sixth under final review.

item.title: China says it met Phase One trade deal terms, warns US against new tariffs
item.description:
China's Commerce Ministry on Tuesday asserted that Beijing has fulfilled its obligations under the 2020 Phase One trade agreement and urged Washington not to use an ongoing Section 301 investigation as a pretext for imposing new tariffs. The statement adds a layer of tension to the bilateral relationship just weeks before President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit Beijing from March 31 to April 2.

A ministry spokesperson said China had "upheld the spirit of the contract" despite pandemic-related disruptions and "faithfully fulfilled" its commitments on intellectual property protections, financial and agricultural market openings, and trade cooperation. The spokesperson warned the United States to "view the Phase One agreement's implementation objectively and rationally," adding that Washington "should not shift blame" and "must not exploit opportunities to create problems".

item.title: Trump demands Iran renounce nuclear weapons ahead of Geneva talks Thursday
item.description: The United States and Iran are set to meet Thursday in Geneva for a third round of indirect nuclear negotiations, talks that U.S. officials have described as perhaps the last chance for a diplomatic resolution before Washington turns to military force. The meeting comes as President Trump, in his State of the Union address Tuesday evening, declared he would "never allow the world's number one sponsor of terror" to possess a nuclear weapon.

item.title: Modi arrives in Israel for historic state visit
item.description:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Israel on February 25 for a two-day state visit, greeted on the tarmac at Ben Gurion Airport by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a scene that echoed their first encounter during Modi's landmark 2017 trip. The visit, Modi's second to Israel and his first since beginning a third term in office, comes at a moment of heightened volatility in the region, as the United States escalates its military posture toward Iran and diplomatic efforts over Tehran's nuclear program remain unresolved.

The trip is designed to deepen cooperation in defense, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and cybersecurity, with a series of bilateral agreements expected to be signed on February 26. But it also places India at the center of a broader geopolitical contest, as Netanyahu seeks to draw New Delhi into a proposed alliance of nations aimed at confronting what he called "radical axes" in the Middle East.

item.title: Uber unveils air taxi booking with Joby in Dubai
item.description:
Uber Technologies and Joby Aviation on Wednesday unveiled "Uber Air powered by Joby," giving riders a first look at how they will be able to book an all-electric air taxi directly through the Uber app. Joby expects to carry its first passengers later this year in Dubai, where it holds a six-year exclusive agreement with the emirate's Roads and Transport Authority to operate air taxi services.

The announcement marks one of the most concrete steps yet in the long-running effort to bring electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft into mainstream urban transportation.

item.title: Canada sends $8M in food aid to Cuba amid U.S. fuel blockade
item.description:
Canada announced on Wednesday it will provide $8 million Canadian (approximately US$6.7 million) in food assistance to Cuba, as Mexico dispatched a second shipment of humanitarian supplies to the island, where an intensifying U.S. fuel blockade has triggered what the United Nations has called a looming "humanitarian collapse."

The twin announcements mark a growing international response to Cuba's deepening crisis, which has left millions of people facing prolonged blackouts, dwindling food supplies, and the near-total collapse of transportation on the Caribbean island of 11 million.

item.title: Zimbabwe halts all raw mineral and lithium exports
item.description:
Zimbabwe on Wednesday suspended exports of all raw minerals and lithium concentrates with immediate effect, a sweeping move that tightens state control over resources critical to global clean-energy supply chains and accelerates the southern African nation's push for domestic processing.

Mines and Mining Development Minister Polite Kambamura announced the ban at a press conference in Harare, stating that the suspension applies to all minerals currently in transit and will remain in place until further notice. "Government expects cooperation of the mining industry on this measure which has been taken in the national interest," Kambamura said, according to the ministry's official statement.

item.title: Witkoff says U.S. demands any Iran nuclear deal last indefinitely
item.description:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff told a private gathering of AIPAC donors in Washington on Tuesday that the Trump administration is insisting any nuclear deal with Iran include no sunset clause, according to a report by Axios citing a U.S. official and two other people familiar with his remarks.

"We go to the Iranians with the understanding that there will be no sunset provision," Witkoff said, according to Axios. "Regardless of whether a deal is achieved, our position is clear: you must adhere to these terms for life."

The demand, made just two days before the next round of U.S.-Iran talks scheduled for Thursday in Geneva, marks a direct attempt to address what President Trump and other critics have long called the central flaw of the 2015 nuclear agreement brokered by the Obama administration. Under that deal, known as the JCPOA, most restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities were set to expire between eight and 25 years after signing.

item.title: Trump speaks with Zelenskyy as Geneva talks set for Thursday
item.description: President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday, Axios reported, as the two sides work to lay the groundwork for a fresh round of trilateral negotiations with Russia expected in early March. The call came one day after Trump told Congress that his administration is "working very hard" to end the war in Ukraine, where he said "25,000 soldiers are dying each and every month."

item.title: Cuba kills four on Florida speedboat in firefight
item.description: Cuba's coast guard shot dead four people and injured six others aboard a U.S.-registered speedboat in an exchange of fire off the island's northern coast on Wednesday morning, the country's Interior Ministry said. The deadly confrontation comes amid a period of intense friction between Washington and Havana over a U.S.-backed oil embargo that has crippled the Cuban economy.

item.title: Spanish scientists build solar panel that also harvests rain energy
item.description: A team of scientists in Seville has created a hybrid device that generates electricity from sunlight and rain simultaneously, turning one of renewable energy's persistent headaches — bad weather — into an additional power source. The work, published in the journal Nano Energy, introduces a thin protective film that shields fragile perovskite solar cells from moisture while also converting the kinetic energy of falling raindrops into electric current.

item.title: AI models used nuclear weapons in 95% of war games, study finds
item.description:
Leading AI systems from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google chose to deploy nuclear weapons in 20 of 21 simulated geopolitical crises, according to new research from King's College London that raises pointed questions about the role of artificial intelligence in military decision-making.

The study, authored by Kenneth Payne and published on the preprint server arXiv on February 16, tested three frontier large language models — OpenAI's GPT-5.2, Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4, and Google's Gemini 3 Flash — in a series of war games involving territorial disputes, competition over scarce resources, and regime survival scenarios. Over 329 turns across the 21 games, the models generated roughly 780,000 words of strategic reasoning. In none of the simulations did any model choose to surrender or fully accommodate its adversary.

"The nuclear taboo doesn't seem to be as powerful for machines as for humans," Payne told New Scientist.

item.title: DeepSeek shuts out Nvidia, AMD from new AI model
item.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence lab DeepSeek has broken with standard industry practice by excluding American chipmakers, including Nvidia and AMD, from early access to its upcoming flagship V4 model, according to a Reuters exclusive citing two sources familiar with the matter.

Instead, DeepSeek granted domestic suppliers, including Huawei Technologies, a head start of several weeks to optimize software for their processors ahead of the model's expected release.

item.title: Canada, South Korea sign military intel-sharing pact
item.description:
Canada and South Korea signed a defense agreement on Wednesday focused on the exchange and protection of classified military information, as Ottawa looks to deepen ties with like-minded middle powers and Seoul positions itself to win a multibillion-dollar Canadian submarine contract.

The signing took place during the second Canada-Republic of Korea Foreign and Defence (2+2) Ministerial Meeting in Ottawa, where Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with their South Korean counterparts, Defence Minister Ahn Gyuback and Foreign Minister Cho Hyun.

item.title: Tropical flowers blooming weeks later due to climate change, study finds
item.description:
Tropical plants are flowering weeks or even months earlier or later than they once did as a result of climate change, according to a study of more than 8,000 plant specimens collected over two centuries. The findings, published on February 25, 2026 in the journal PLOS One, challenge the long-held assumption that tropical ecosystems — home to more than half the world's plant biodiversity — are insulated from the phenological disruptions already documented in temperate and boreal regions.

Researchers Skylar Graves and Erin Manzitto-Tripp of the University of Colorado-Boulder analyzed museum herbarium specimens representing 33 tropical species with distinct annual flowering periods, collected between 1794 and 2024 from sites in Brazil, Ecuador, Peru, Ghana, Guinea, Thailand, and Bolivia. They found that flowering periods have shifted by an average of about two days per decade.
